Ford Madox Brown was born in Calais, France, to English parents and trained in Belgium before settling in London. He was a close friend of the Pre-Raphaelites, though he never formally joined them. He painted history, literature and scenes of modern working life, including the famous 'Work'. He died in London in 1893.

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was born into a noble family in Albi, France, but broken bones in childhood stunted his growth. He moved to Montmartre in Paris and painted the dancers, singers and cabaret stars of the Moulin Rouge. His bold posters helped invent modern advertising art. He died at 36, at his mother's château in southwestern France.

Paul Delaroche was born in Paris and became one of France's most popular painters of dramatic history scenes. He worked and taught in Paris, where he trained many future artists. His paintings often show famous tragedies, such as the death of royalty. He died in Paris in 1856.

Mary Cassatt was born near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and moved to Paris as a young woman. She was the only American to join the French Impressionists, and she specialized in tender pictures of mothers and children. She lived in France most of her life, and she also encouraged American collectors to buy Impressionist art. She died at her country home in France in 1926.

François Boucher was born in Paris and became the favorite painter of Madame de Pompadour, the French king's companion. He lived in Paris and was the leading figure in the Rococo style, with its pastel colors and playful, romantic scenes. He painted, designed tapestries and decorated palaces. He died in Paris in 1770.

Edvard Munch was born in Norway and grew up in Christiania (now Oslo), in a family troubled by illness and loss. He traveled in Europe, especially Germany and France, and used paint to express anxiety, love and loneliness. His most famous work, 'The Scream', is among the best-known images ever. He spent his last decades at his estate Ekely near Oslo and died in 1944.

Egon Schiele was born in Tulln, Austria, and studied art in Vienna as a teenager. He was inspired by Gustav Klimt and developed a raw, angular and expressive drawing style. He lived in Vienna and in smaller Austrian towns. He died of the Spanish flu in 1918 at just 28, three days after his wife.

William Holman Hunt was born in London and, with Millais and Rossetti, founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848. He traveled to the Middle East to paint biblical scenes with realistic backgrounds. His most famous painting is 'The Light of the World'. He died in London in 1910.

Mikhail Vrubel was born in Omsk, Siberia, and studied in Saint Petersburg. He lived in Russia and Ukraine, creating glittering, mosaic-like paintings and designs for theaters. He is best known for paintings of the Demon, a moody figure from a Russian poem. He lost his sight in later life and died in Saint Petersburg in 1910.

Edward Burne-Jones was born in Birmingham, England, and moved to London to become an artist. He was part of the second wave of Pre-Raphaelites and also designed stained glass and tapestries with William Morris. His dreamy paintings were inspired by medieval legends and myths. He was made a baronet and died in London in 1898.

George Frederic Watts was born in London and trained as a sculptor and painter. He painted portraits of the great and the good, as well as symbolic works on big themes like Hope and Love. In his later years he lived in the English village of Compton, where his gallery still stands. He died in 1904.

Adolph Tidemand was born in Mandal, Norway, and trained in Copenhagen and Düsseldorf. He lived much of his life in Germany and Norway, painting scenes of Norwegian farmers and folk traditions. He helped create the image of Norwegian national identity in the 1800s. He died in Christiania in 1876.

Hans Gude was born in Christiania (Oslo), Norway, and spent much of his career in Germany. He was a star of Norwegian landscape painting, depicting mountains, fjords and coasts. He taught in Düsseldorf and Berlin and trained many painters. He died in Berlin in 1903.

Frederic Edwin Church was born in Hartford, Connecticut, and studied with Thomas Cole. He traveled to South America, the Arctic and the Middle East, painting giant landscapes full of wonder. He became one of the most famous artists in the United States. He built a Persian-style mansion called Olana on the Hudson River.

Thomas Eakins was born in Philadelphia and lived there nearly all his life. He studied anatomy and photography so his paintings of people, rowers and surgeons would be true to life. His honest realism upset some people, but is now praised. He taught art in Philadelphia and died there in 1916.

Dante Gabriel Rossetti was born in London to an Italian family of poets and scholars. He co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood and painted dreamy, romantic women. He was also a poet, and often paired paintings with verses. He lived in London and died in 1882.

John Trumbull was born in Lebanon, Connecticut, and served as an officer in the American Revolution. Afterwards he studied painting in London with Benjamin West. He is best known for paintings of key events in the Revolution, such as the signing of the Declaration of Independence. He died in New York City in 1843.

Henri Matisse was born in northern France and began painting after an illness at age 20. He lived in Paris and then in Nice in the south, where he painted in bold, free colors. He was the leader of Fauvism, whose name means 'wild beasts', and later made colorful paper cut-outs. He died in Nice in 1954.

Vasily Vereshchagin was born in Cherepovets, Russia, and traveled to Central Asia, India and the Balkans. He painted battlefields to show the true horror of war, sometimes as a war correspondent. His anti-war art shocked many viewers. He died in 1904 when a warship he was aboard struck a mine.

Joaquín Sorolla was born in Valencia, Spain, and became known as the 'master of light' for his sparkling paintings of beaches and sunshine. He worked in Madrid and traveled to Paris and the United States, where he was very popular. His house in Madrid is now a museum. He died in Spain in 1923.

Aleksander Gierymski was born in Warsaw, Poland, and studied in Germany and Italy. He painted moonlit city scenes, with great honesty about everyday life. He lived in Warsaw and later in Rome, where he spent his last years. He died in 1901.

Rosa Bonheur was born in Bordeaux, France, and grew up in Paris, where she studied animals at farms and markets. She became one of the most famous women artists of the 1800s, painting horses, cattle and sheep. She even got official permission to wear trousers in public so she could work. She died at her château in Thomery, near Paris, in 1899.

Frédéric Bazille was born into a wealthy family in Montpellier, France, and moved to Paris to paint. He was a close friend of Monet and Renoir and shared a studio with them. He painted sunny outdoor scenes and portraits. He was killed in the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 when he was only 28.

Marguerite Gérard was born in Grasse, France, and moved to Paris as a teenager to train with her brother-in-law, Fragonard. She became a successful painter of elegant home scenes, often showing women reading, writing or playing music. She exhibited at the Salon and sold to the wealthy collectors of Europe. She died in Paris in 1837.

Antoine-Jean Gros was born in Paris and was a student of Jacques-Louis David. He became Napoleon's war painter, traveling with the army to capture battles and heroic scenes. His lively, dramatic art influenced the Romantic painters. He died in 1835 near Paris.

Arnold Böcklin was born in Basel, Switzerland, and spent long periods in Italy and Germany. He painted dreamy scenes full of myths, strange creatures and mysterious islands. He is best known for 'Isle of the Dead'. He died near Florence in 1901.

John Singleton Copley was born in Boston and became America's finest portrait painter before the Revolution. He painted merchants and patriots, like Paul Revere. In 1774 he moved to England as war loomed, and spent the rest of his life in London. He died there in 1815.

Henry Raeburn was born in Stockbridge, near Edinburgh, Scotland, and became Scotland's best-known portrait painter. He painted writers, lawyers and clan chiefs with a lively, confident brush. He was knighted in 1822. He lived and worked in Edinburgh until his death in 1823.

Alexander Ivanov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, and spent nearly 20 years in Rome working on one giant painting, 'The Appearance of Christ to the People'. He made hundreds of studies for it. He returned to Russia shortly before his death in 1858. His art deeply influenced Russian painters.

Carl Bloch was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, and became one of the country's most beloved painters of history and religious scenes. He spent years studying in Italy. His pictures of Bible stories are reproduced all over the world. He died in Copenhagen in 1890.

Thomas Cole was born in England and moved to the United States as a teenager, settling near the Hudson River in New York. He founded the Hudson River School, a group of artists who painted America's wild landscapes. His paintings often carried messages about nature and civilization. He died in Catskill, New York, in 1848.

Paul Émile Chabas was born in Nantes, France, and became a popular painter in Paris. He is best known for dreamy paintings of young people by lakes and meadows in soft light. His work was admired by the public in the early 1900s. He died in Paris in 1937.

Piet Mondrian was born in the Netherlands and started out painting windmills and trees. He lived in Amsterdam, Paris, London and finally New York City. Over time he simplified his art into straight black lines and blocks of red, yellow and blue. He died in New York in 1944, and his style inspired architects and designers worldwide.

Vasily Surikov was born in Krasnoyarsk, in Siberia, and moved to Moscow and Saint Petersburg. He painted huge history scenes of Russia's past with crowds of vivid individuals. His paintings are among Russia's most loved. He died in Moscow in 1916.

William Etty was born in York, England, and spent his life training to paint like the Old Masters. He is best known for his rich colors and glowing skin tones. He worked in London but retired to his hometown of York. He died there in 1849.

Paul Klee was born near Bern, Switzerland, to a musical family and was also a talented violinist. He taught at the Bauhaus, a famous art school in Germany, and later fled the Nazis to Switzerland. His playful, imaginative paintings use lines, colors and symbols as if they were music. He died in Switzerland in 1940.

Umberto Boccioni was born in Reggio Calabria, Italy, and became the leader of Futurism, a movement that celebrated speed and machines. He worked in Milan and Rome, painting and making sculptures full of motion. He died at 33 after falling from a horse during military training in 1916.

Jean-Étienne Liotard was born in Geneva, Switzerland, and traveled across Europe and to Constantinople. He is best known for pastel portraits with a precise, glowing look. He worked for royals and nobles in Vienna, Paris and England. He died in Geneva in 1789.

Gustave Moreau was born in Paris and became a leading Symbolist painter. He painted glittering scenes from myth and the Bible, with fantastic detail. He later taught at the École des Beaux-Arts, where Matisse was a student. His Paris house is now a museum.

Giuseppe Pellizza da Volpedo was born in Volpedo, in northern Italy, and lived there much of his life. He painted in the style of dots and fine brushstrokes of pointillism. His masterpiece 'The Fourth Estate' shows workers marching for their rights. He died in 1907 at age 39.

P. S. Krøyer was born in Stavanger, Norway, and grew up in Copenhagen, Denmark. He was the central figure of the Skagen Painters, an artist colony in northern Denmark. His paintings capture the beautiful blue light of summer evenings by the sea. He died in Skagen in 1909.

Alexei Savrasov was born in Moscow and taught at the Moscow School of Painting. His painting 'The Rooks Have Returned' is often seen as the start of the Russian landscape tradition. He painted ordinary rural scenes with deep feeling. He died in Moscow in 1897.

Viktor Vasnetsov was born in a village in northern Russia, the son of a priest. He lived in Moscow, and became known for painting scenes from Russian folk tales and legends, with warriors, witches and firebirds. He also designed churches and theater sets. He died in Moscow in 1926.

Paul Baudry was born in La Roche-sur-Yon, France, and trained in Paris and Rome. He painted elegant portraits and murals, including the ceiling of the Paris Opera foyer. His work was admired by the Emperor Napoleon III. He died in Paris in 1886.

Johann Zoffany was born in Frankfurt, Germany, and moved to London. He painted 'conversation pieces' — groups of people in rooms and gardens — as well as theatrical scenes. He traveled to Italy and India, and became a favorite of the British royal family. He died in London in 1810.

Franz von Stuck was born in Bavaria, Germany, and became a celebrated painter and teacher in Munich. He was a founding member of the Munich Secession and painted mysterious and powerful symbolic pictures. Kandinsky and Klee were among his students. He lived in a grand villa in Munich, which is now a museum.

John Collier was born in London and studied art in London, Paris and Munich. He painted portraits and scenes from history and legend, often with strong feelings. He also wrote about art and science. He died in London in 1934.

Alexander Roslin was born in Malmö, Sweden, and became a leading portrait painter at the French court. He lived in Paris, where he painted queens, kings and the leading minds of the day. His specialty was the shimmer of silks and satins. He died in Paris in 1793.

Giuseppe Castiglione was born in Milan, Italy, and became a Jesuit brother, traveling as a missionary to China. He took the name Lang Shining and served as a court painter for three Chinese emperors. He blended European realism with Chinese styles. He died in Beijing in 1766.

Herbert James Draper was born in London and studied at the Royal Academy. He painted scenes from Greek and Roman myth with glowing color and graceful figures. His 'The Lament for Icarus' is his best-known work. He died in London in 1920.

Wassily Kandinsky was born in Moscow and trained as a lawyer before becoming a painter at age 30. He lived in Russia, Germany and later France. He is considered one of the first artists to paint truly abstract works, using color and shape like music. He died in Neuilly-sur-Seine, near Paris, in 1944.

Benjamin West was born near Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and moved to Europe in his twenties. He settled in London, where he became the history painter to King George III and later President of the Royal Academy. He taught many American painters. He died in London in 1820.
